colosseo: The Flavian Amphitheatre seen from outside, with the Arch of Constantine beside it, then Via dei Fori Imperiali, the wide avenue lined with the remains of the Forums of Caesar, Augustus and Trajan.
campidoglio: Piazza Venezia and the Capitoline Hill

The Altare della Patria (the "Vittoriano", which Italians jokingly call "the typewriter"), then Michelangelo's staircase up to Piazza del Campidoglio. Behind Palazzo Senatorio there's a viewpoint over the Roman Forum.
pantheon: The best-preserved Roman temple, still with its original dome and the round opening at the top that lets in the light (and, when it rains, the water). Inside are the tombs of Raphael and the kings of Italy.
navona: Piazza Navona and Campo de' Fiori
The oval square on Domitian's old stadium, with Bernini's Fountain of the Four Rivers, then the lanes to Campo de' Fiori, where there's a market in the morning.
trevi: Rome's largest Baroque fountain, filling an entire palace façade. Toss a coin with your right hand, your back to the fountain: whoever does will return to Rome.
spagna: Spanish Steps and Trinità dei Monti
Bernini's Barcaccia fountain at the foot of the 135 steps that climb to the church of Trinità dei Monti: from the terrace at the top you can see Rome's rooftops all the way to the dome of St Peter's.
sanpietro: Bernini's colonnade and the square, then the largest church in the world: Michelangelo's Pietà, the bronze canopy and the dome. There's a security check at the entrance.
trastevere: Ivy-covered lanes, Piazza di Santa Maria in Trastevere with the basilica's golden mosaics, and the neighbourhood streets down to Piazza Trilussa.
ghetto: Jewish Ghetto, Portico d'Ottavia and Tiber Island
The Jewish quarter, the oldest in Europe, with the ruins of the Portico d'Ottavia, the Turtle Fountain and the Tiber with Tiber Island.
colosseoins: Inside the amphitheatre, on the arena and the upper levels; then the Roman Forum with the Via Sacra and the Arch of Titus, and the Palatine, the hill of the imperial palaces, overlooking the Circus Maximus.
vaticani: A mile of galleries: the Gallery of Maps, the Raphael Rooms with the "School of Athens" and, at the end, the Sistine Chapel with Michelangelo's Last Judgement.
castel: Emperor Hadrian's mausoleum turned papal fortress: ramps, frescoed apartments and, at the top, a terrace with views over all of Rome. In front is Ponte Sant'Angelo with its angel statues.
gianicolo: The terrace on the hill above Trastevere, with the widest view of Rome: the dome of St Peter's, the Pantheon and the hills beyond. On the way you pass the Acqua Paola Fountain, the "Fontanone".
borghese: Cardinal Scipione Borghese's collection: Bernini's Rape of Proserpina and Apollo and Daphne, Canova's Paolina Borghese, and paintings by Caravaggio and Raphael. Exactly two hours.
pincio: Villa Borghese, Pincio and Piazza del Popolo
Rome's great park: tree-lined avenues, the pond of the Giardino del Lago and the Pincio Terrace, overlooking the whole of Piazza del Popolo and, at sunset, the city's pink rooftops.
aventino: Aventine: Orange Garden and the Keyhole

On the Aventine Hill, the Orange Garden with its viewpoint over the Tiber and St Peter's. A little further on, the square of the Knights of Malta: through the keyhole of the gate you see the dome of St Peter's framed by greenery.
bocca: Mouth of Truth and Circus Maximus
The stone mask in the portico of Santa Maria in Cosmedin, which legend says bites the hand of liars, and the nearby Circus Maximus, the huge meadow where chariots once raced.
caracalla: Emperor Caracalla's enormous public baths (3rd century): walls dozens of metres high, mosaics and the underground rooms where thousands of slaves worked.
testaccio: The former slaughterhouse district, home of Rome's traditional working-class cooking: the covered market with its sandwich stalls (porchetta, tripe), streets of local trattorias and Monte Testaccio, a hill made of broken amphorae.
